title: Sew a Button, Mend a Seam
bigQuestion: Why fix a piece of clothing instead of throwing it away?

story.title: The Coat on the Coldest Day
story.kicker: One missing button, a wind off the lake, and ten minutes with a needle.
paragraphs: It was the coldest morning of the year in Chicago. The wind came off the lake and cut through everything. Devon pulled on his winter coat and reached for the top button. It was gone. There was just a loose tuft of thread where it used to be.

"Wear it open," his sister said. But the cold went straight down his neck at the bus stop. All day the coat flapped. At recess he held it shut with one hand and could not play. He came home cross and cold.

His dad found the button in the pocket. "Ten minutes," he said, and got out the sewing box. He picked heavy thread that matched the coat. He threaded a needle and tied a knot three times, because coat cloth is thick.

He showed Devon how to hold the button a little away from the coat, with a toothpick under it. He stitched up through one hole and down through the other, six times. Then he wrapped the thread around and around under the button. "That is the shank," he said. "It gives the buttonhole room."

Devon tied it off himself. He buttoned the coat to the top. The button sat proud and firm. A new coat would have cost a lot of money. This fix cost a piece of thread and ten minutes, and the coat was warm again.
story.think: Devon's dad said the shank gives the buttonhole room. What do you think would happen if the button were sewn flat and tight against the thick coat?

lessons.title: Two Holes and Four
lessons.mainIdea: Buttons come with two holes or four holes, and you sew through the holes in a pattern that matches the other buttons.
reading: Look at the buttons on your shirt. Some have two holes. Some have four. A *two-hole button* is sewn with the thread going up one hole and down the other, over and over. It makes one short bar of thread on top.

A *four-hole button* can be sewn two ways. Two straight bars, like an equals sign. Or two crossed bars, like an X. Look at the other buttons on the same shirt and copy their pattern. A button that does not match looks like a patch.

Some buttons have no holes at all. They have a little loop on the back called a shank. You sew through the loop. Before you start, hold the button up to the buttonhole. It should slide through with a small push. Too big and it will not close. Too small and it slips open.

words.d: a button with two holes; the thread goes up one and down the other
a button with four holes, sewn as two bars or as an X
the small slit in the cloth that the button pushes through

look.title: Copy the Pattern
look.text: A shirt has six four-hole buttons. Five of them are sewn with two straight bars, like an equals sign. The sixth is missing. In the button jar there is a four-hole button the same size and a two-hole button a little bigger.
look.prompt: Which button should you choose and how should you sew it so it matches the other five?

check.q: A four-hole button can be sewn in which two patterns?
check.why: Four holes can be stitched as two straight bars or as crossed bars.

check.q: Why should you check the button against the buttonhole first?
choices: To see that it fits through with a small push
check.why: A button that is too big will not close; one that is too small slips open.

check.q: How should a replacement button be sewn on a shirt?
choices: In the same pattern as the other buttons
check.why: Matching the pattern of the other buttons keeps the shirt looking right.

lessons.title: The Thread Shank
lessons.mainIdea: A shank is a short stem of thread under the button that leaves room for the cloth of the buttonhole.
reading: Button a shirt. Look at how the button sits. The cloth of the buttonhole slides under it. A button sewn flat and tight has no room for that cloth. It pulls, puckers, and pops off. A button with a *shank* sits a little above the cloth on a stem of thread.

To make a shank, place a toothpick or a matchstick across the top of the button before you stitch. Sew over it. When you are done, pull the stick out. The button now has a little slack under it. Wrap the thread around that slack five or six times to make a firm stem.

Thick cloth needs a longer shank. A coat needs more room than a thin shirt. For a thin shirt, one toothpick is enough. For a coat, use two sticks or a *bulkier* stick. The rule: the shank should be about as tall as the cloth is thick.

words.d: the short stem of thread under a button that leaves room for the buttonhole cloth
thicker; a bulkier stick makes a taller shank for thick cloth

look.title: The Button That Popped Off Again
look.text: Nia sewed a button back onto her winter coat. She pulled every stitch as tight as she could so it would never fall off. The button was flat against the coat. The first time she buttoned it, the cloth puckered. By Friday the button had popped off again.
look.prompt: What was missing from Nia's button? What should she put under the button next time, and how many?

check.q: What does the shank do?
choices: Leaves room for the buttonhole cloth under the button
check.why: The stem of thread lets the buttonhole cloth slide under the button without pulling.

check.q: How do you make a shank?
choices: Sew the button as tight as you can
Sew over a toothpick, then pull it out and wrap the thread
check.why: The toothpick leaves slack; wrapping the thread turns the slack into a firm stem.

check.q: Which needs the longer shank?
check.why: The shank should be about as tall as the cloth is thick, and coat cloth is thickest.

lessons.title: Sewing the Button On
lessons.mainIdea: Mark the spot, anchor the thread, stitch through the holes six times, wrap the shank, and tie off on the back.
reading: Find the spot. Button the other buttons and see where the loose buttonhole lands. Mark that spot with a pin or a dot of chalk. Thread a needle with strong thread. For a button, tie the knot two or three times, or use the thread *doubled* so it is twice as strong.

Bring the needle up from the wrong side at the mark. Slide the button on. Lay a toothpick across the top. Go down the other hole and back up. Do this six times for a two-hole button. For four holes, do three times through each pair.

Pull out the toothpick. Lift the button gently. Bring the needle out between the button and the cloth. Wrap the thread around the stem five or six times. Push the needle to the back. Tie two finishing knots and snip. Tug the button. It should be firm, with a little wiggle from the shank.

words.d: thread pulled through the eye until both ends are even, so you sew with two strands at once
a pin or chalk dot showing exactly where the button goes

look.title: Order the Button Steps
look.text: Here are the button steps, mixed up. Wrap the thread under the button. Mark the spot. Stitch through the holes six times over a toothpick. Tie off on the back. Thread the needle and knot it. Bring the needle up from the wrong side.
look.prompt: Put the six steps in order. Which step comes right before you slide the button on?

check.q: How do you find where the missing button goes?
choices: Button the others and see where the empty buttonhole lands
Put it next to the pocket
check.why: The buttonhole shows exactly where the button must sit.

check.q: Why sew with doubled thread for a button?
choices: Two strands are twice as strong
check.why: Buttons get pulled a lot. Doubled thread holds better.

check.q: About how many times do you stitch through a two-hole button?
check.why: Six passes make a button firm without a bulky pile of thread.

lessons.title: A Split Seam
lessons.mainIdea: A split seam is a seam where the old thread broke, and you fix it from the inside with a back stitch over the old stitch line.
reading: You bend over and hear a rip. The seam on the side of your shirt has split. The cloth is not torn. The old thread just broke or wore out. This is the easiest repair there is. You put new thread where the old thread was.

Turn the shirt *inside out* so the wrong side is facing you. Find the old stitch line. It is a faint line of tiny holes, with the old thread still on both sides of the gap. Pin the two edges together along that line so they match.

Start your new stitches about a finger-width before the gap, on top of the old stitches that still hold. Use the *back stitch* along the old line through the gap. Go a finger-width past the other end. Tie off. Turn it right side out. The fix is hidden inside.

words.d: a seam that has opened because the old thread broke, while the cloth is not torn
turned so the wrong side faces you and the seam is easy to reach
the strong locked stitch used for seams that get pulled

look.title: Where to Start?
look.text: Inside a shirt, wrong side out. The side seam has a gap about as long as a finger. On both sides of the gap the old stitches are still there. One student wants to start stitching right at the edge of the gap. Another wants to start a little before the gap, on top of the old stitches.
look.prompt: Which student is right, and why? What could happen if you start right at the edge of the gap?

check.q: What is a split seam?
choices: The thread broke and the seam opened
The cloth has a hole in the middle
check.why: In a split seam the cloth is fine; the old stitches gave way.

check.q: How should the shirt be turned to fix a seam?
check.why: Inside out puts the wrong side and the old stitch line in front of you.

check.q: Where do you start the new stitches?
choices: In the middle of the gap
A little before the gap, on the old stitches
check.why: Overlapping the old stitches locks the new seam to the part that still holds.

lessons.title: Pin It So It Matches
lessons.mainIdea: Before you mend, pin the two edges so they line up exactly, or the seam will pucker or twist.
reading: Two edges of a split seam do not stay together on their own. If one slides while you sew, the seam ends up twisted. One side gets longer than the other. The shirt puckers. Pins stop this.

Lay the two edges flat, wrong side up. Match the old stitch lines. Push a pin *across* the seam line, not along it, about every two finger-widths. Pins across the line are easy to pull out as the needle gets close.

Sew up to each pin. Pull it out just before the needle reaches it. Never sew over a pin. The needle can hit it and bend, or the pin can get sewn in. When you finish, count your pins. Every pin goes back in the *pincushion*.

words.d: pinned at a right angle to the seam line, so pins are easy to remove as you sew
where every pin returns after the seam is sewn

look.title: The Twisted Seam
look.text: Malik fixed the seam on a pillowcase without pinning. He held the edges with his fingers. By the end, one edge stuck out a thumb-width past the other. The seam looks like a wave, and the pillowcase does not lie flat.
look.prompt: What should Malik have done before the first stitch? How far apart would you put the pins?

check.q: Why pin the edges before mending a seam?
choices: So the edges do not slide and twist
check.why: Pins hold the two edges lined up so the seam stays straight.

check.q: Which way do the pins go?
check.why: Pins across the line are easy to pull out as the needle gets close.

check.q: What do you do when your needle reaches a pin?
check.why: Sewing over a pin can bend the needle or trap the pin in the seam.

lessons.title: Make Clothes Last
lessons.mainIdea: Small habits, such as hanging, folding, washing gently and fixing early, make clothes last for years.
reading: A tiny loose thread on a seam is a one-minute fix today. In a month it is a split seam that is a ten-minute fix. Left longer, the edges fray and the shirt is hard to save. Fix small problems early. Check pockets and seams when you put clothes away.

How you wash matters too. Read the small *care label* inside the collar. It says whether to wash cold or warm and whether the dryer is okay. Hot water and a hot dryer can shrink some cloth and fade colors. Zip zippers and empty pockets before washing.

Hang or fold clothes instead of dropping them. Wear the right clothes for the job; play clothes for mud. A loose button gets sewn tight before it falls off and gets lost. These habits are free. They keep clothes *wearable* for years.

words.d: the small tag inside clothing that tells how to wash and dry it
in good enough shape to wear

look.title: Read the Tag
look.text: Inside the collar of a sweater, a tag reads: Wash cold. Do not bleach. Lay flat to dry. Ana wants to throw it in a hot wash with towels and then into the dryer on high so it will be ready fast.
look.prompt: Which of Ana's plans go against the tag? What could happen to the sweater?

check.q: When is the best time to fix a loose thread on a seam?
choices: Right away, while it is a small job
check.why: A small fix now stops a bigger split later.

check.q: Where do you find how to wash a piece of clothing?
check.why: The care label tells the water temperature and whether to use the dryer.

check.q: What can hot water and a hot dryer do to some clothes?
check.why: Heat can shrink some cloth and fade colors, so follow the label.

lessons.title: A Felt Bookmark
lessons.mainIdea: A felt bookmark is a first project that uses cutting, a running stitch and a finishing knot.
reading: Felt is a good first cloth. It does not fray at the edges, and it comes in bright colors. Cut a strip of *felt* about 2 inches wide and 6 inches long. Use a ruler and mark the corners with chalk before you cut, so the sides are straight.

Cut a small shape from a second color: a heart, a star, a leaf. Pin it to the strip. Thread a needle with a color that shows. Sew around the shape with a *running stitch*, small and even. The stitches are part of the design, so make them neat.

Tie off on the back with two knots. Snip the tail. Now sew a line of running stitch all around the edge of the strip, a finger-width in from the edge. That is the border. Tie off, snip, count your pins. You made a bookmark from two scraps.

words.d: a thick soft cloth that does not fray when cut, good for first projects
the in-and-out stitch used here as decoration and to hold the shape

look.title: Bookmark Cut List (example)
look.cite: Example cut list for a felt bookmark
look.prompt: If the border sits half an inch in from each edge, how wide is the space inside the border on a 2-inch strip?

check.q: Why is felt a good cloth for a first project?
choices: It does not fray at the cut edges
check.why: Cut felt edges stay neat, so you can skip hemming.

check.q: What do you do before you cut the strip?
choices: Measure with a ruler and mark the corners
check.why: Marking first keeps the cut straight.

check.q: Which stitch goes around the shape and the border?
check.why: A small, even running stitch holds the shape and looks like a design.

lessons.title: A Felt Pouch
lessons.mainIdea: Fold a rectangle of felt, back stitch the two sides, and you have a pouch that holds coins or pencils.
reading: Cut a *rectangle* of felt 4 inches wide and 10 inches long. Fold it so the short ends meet, but leave one end about 2 inches longer than the other. The longer end will become the flap. Pin the two sides.

Sew each side with the back stitch, a finger-width in from the edge. This pouch will carry things and get opened and closed a lot, so it needs the strong stitch. Start and end each side with knots. Pull the pins as you go.

Fold the *flap* over the front. If you want, sew a button on the front and cut a small slit in the flap for a buttonhole. Snip only as long as the button is wide. Now you have a pouch. Every step used a skill from this unit.

words.d: a four-sided shape with square corners, like the felt piece you cut
the extra piece of felt that folds over the top to close the pouch

look.title: Plan the Pouch
look.text: A 10-inch strip of felt. You fold it so the front is 4 inches tall and the flap is 2 inches. Amir wonders why the two side seams are done in back stitch when the bookmark was fine with a running stitch.
look.prompt: Explain to Amir why the pouch uses the back stitch. How tall is the back of the pouch?

check.q: Why does the pouch use the back stitch instead of the running stitch?
choices: The pouch gets pulled and opened and needs a strong seam
check.why: Seams that get pulled every day need the locked, gap-free stitch.

check.q: What is the flap?
choices: The extra end that folds over the top
check.why: The longer end folds over the front to close the pouch.

check.q: How long should the buttonhole slit be?
choices: About as long as the button is wide
check.why: A slit the width of the button lets it push through and still hold.

lessons.title: Fix It or Toss It?
lessons.mainIdea: Mending saves money and keeps cloth out of the trash, so fixing usually beats throwing away.
reading: A shirt loses a button. One choice: throw it away and buy a new one. Another choice: sew the button back on. Example: a new shirt costs $15. A spool of thread costs $2 and sews on dozens of buttons. The fix costs a few cents of thread and ten minutes.

Throwing clothes away has a second cost. Thrown-away cloth goes to a *landfill*, a big pile of trash that stays for a very long time. Making new cloth takes water, farms, factories and trucks. A mended shirt means one less shirt made and one less shirt in the pile.

Sometimes a piece really is done. Cloth that is worn thin all over cannot hold a stitch. Then it can become a rag or a scrap for a project. But a split seam, a loose hem or a lost button are small. Ask first: can I fix this? Most of the time, you can.

words.d: a place where trash is buried; thrown-away clothes end up there
to fix a piece of clothing by sewing

look.title: Fix It or Replace It (example)
look.cite: Example prices for comparing a repair to a replacement
look.prompt: If one $2 spool sews on 40 buttons, about how much thread money does one button fix cost? Compare that to a new shirt.

check.q: In the example, what does a new shirt cost compared to fixing one button?
choices: The new shirt costs much more, about $15 to a few cents of thread
check.why: A $2 spool sews many buttons, so one fix is only cents; a new shirt is $15 in the example.

check.q: Where do thrown-away clothes usually end up?
check.why: Trash, including cloth, is buried in a landfill and stays a long time.

check.q: Which piece is probably too worn to mend?
choices: A shirt with one loose button
Cloth worn thin all over that will not hold a stitch
A pouch with a split seam
check.why: Stitches need sound cloth to hold. Thin, worn-out cloth can become rags instead.

review.q: How can a four-hole button be sewn so it matches the others?
choices: In the same pattern as the other buttons
review.why: Copy the pattern, two bars or an X, so the shirt looks right.

review.q: What is the shank under a button for?
choices: To leave room for the buttonhole cloth
review.why: The shank lets the buttonhole cloth slide under without puckering.

review.q: How do you leave room for a shank while you stitch?
choices: Sew over a toothpick, then pull it out
review.why: The toothpick leaves slack that you wrap into a stem.

review.q: How should a shirt be turned to mend a split seam?
review.why: Inside out puts the old stitch line in front of you and hides the fix.

review.q: Which stitch mends a seam that gets pulled every day?
review.why: The back stitch locks each stitch into the last and will not gap open.

review.q: What do you do when your needle reaches a pin?
review.why: Sewing over a pin can bend the needle or sew the pin in.

review.q: Why is felt good for a first project?
choices: Its cut edges do not fray
review.why: Felt edges stay neat when cut, so a beginner can skip hemming.

review.q: Why does mending usually beat throwing away?
choices: Mending costs little and keeps cloth out of the landfill
review.why: A fix costs cents and minutes; a new piece costs dollars and adds to the trash pile.
